identity.title: Reasoning Elicitation in Language Models via Counterfactual Feedback

problem.claim: Language models lack causal reasoning in counterfactual question answering.

gap.claim: Traditional metrics based only on factual accuracy provide a less complete view of language-model reasoning than metrics that also balance counterfactual accuracy.

contributions.claim: The authors derive metrics balancing accuracy on factual and counterfactual questions.
The authors propose several fine-tuning approaches intended to elicit better reasoning mechanisms under the proposed metrics.
The authors evaluate fine-tuned models across realistic scenarios and problems involving inductive and deductive reasoning.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors state that their metrics offer a more complete reasoning assessment than traditional factual-only metrics.

narrative_sequence.summary: The paper frames language-model reasoning as underdeveloped, especially for counterfactual causal question answering.
It states that the work aims to address this gap.
It introduces metrics combining factual and counterfactual accuracy.
It proposes fine-tuning approaches and evaluates them in realistic, generalization-oriented reasoning scenarios.

source_observation.claim: The abstract aligns the proposed fine-tuning approaches with explicitly defined metrics that combine factual and counterfactual performance.

lessons.interpretation: Defining the target measurement before describing the intervention can make the intended claim-evidence relationship explicit.
lessons.application: For a reasoning-method paper, introduce an evaluation metric that reflects the target capability, then state that training changes are assessed against it.
lessons.exception: This is unsuitable when the target capability already has a well-established metric or when combining dimensions obscures important failure modes.

unknowns: The abstract reports no numerical results, baselines, scenario details, or observed generalization outcomes.
It does not specify the exact metric formulas, fine-tuning procedures, model families, or evaluation problems.
The stated metric distinction is author-reported and does not independently establish priority or superiority.
